title: Giant Salvinia in Rice Fields: How to Spot and Remove It
metaTitle: Giant Salvinia in Rice Fields: Identification and Control
metaDescription: Giant salvinia is a floating fern that can cut rice yield by 12.5 percent and passes for azolla. Learn to tell them apart and clear it from your field.
excerpt: Giant salvinia is a hairy floating fern that covers the water of irrigated lowland rice fields with thick green mats. It spread into rice fields because farmers mistook it for azolla. This page shows you how to spot it, how to tell it from azolla, and how to clear it from your field and canals before it spreads.

heroImage.alt: Giant salvinia (Salvinia molesta), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Marshman, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Giant salvinia, or Salvinia molesta, is a floating fern from the family Salviniaceae. It has no local name in the PhilRice weed list, so it goes by its English name or simply salvinia. It floats on still or slow water. In the Philippines, it is a weed of irrigated lowland rice fields, where water stays in the field for most of the season.

It is a perennial and keeps growing as long as it has water. As a fern, it never flowers or makes seeds. Instead, it spreads mainly by broken pieces of stem, and it also forms spores. Moving water and farm tools carry these pieces to new spots. In fact, farmers brought it into rice fields by mistake, thinking it was azolla, the small fern they use as green manure.

Look for a hairy, green mat floating on the water. This plant is a floating fern, not a flowering broadleaf, but its wide, round leaves set it apart from grasses and sedges. Young leaves lie flat and oval. Older leaves turn heart shaped and fold upward. Stiff, spine like hairs cover the top of each leaf. At each node, it carries two green floating leaves and one brown, root like leaf that hangs below.

items: Thick, hairy green mats spreading across still water in the field and canals.
Young leaves flat and oval, older leaves heart shaped and folded upward.
Stiff, spine like hairs on the upper side of each leaf that shed water.
Two green floating leaves and one brown, root like hanging leaf at each node.
Look alike tip: azolla is much smaller, with tiny overlapping scales, and often turns reddish.

blocks.text:
Giant salvinia can reduce rice yield by 12.5 percent. It does this by covering the water with wide, thick mats. These mats block sunlight, crowd young rice and take nutrients from the water.

Mats also clog canals and drains, so water moves slowly into and out of your field. The worst part is how it got in. It spread into rice fields because farmers mistook it for azolla and moved it on purpose. So check every batch of azolla before you bring it to your field.

items: Scoop out mats with a net or basket while they are small. Leave no pieces behind, since each fragment can grow into a new plant.
Check any azolla before you bring it in. Real azolla is tiny and scaly, while salvinia has bigger, hairy, folded leaves.
Clean canals and inlets, and set a net or screen where water enters your field to catch drifting pieces.
Pile removed plants on high, dry ground far from water so they dry out completely.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold giant salvinia down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Giant Salvinia Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Giant Salvinia?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Giant Salvinia

items.q: What is giant salvinia commonly called?
items.a: It has no local name in the PhilRice weed list. Most people use its English name, or simply salvinia, from its scientific name Salvinia molesta. Some farmers mistake it for azolla, but they are different ferns. Azolla helps rice as green manure, while this one only spreads and competes with your crop.

items.q: How do I get rid of salvinia in my rice field?
items.a: Prevention comes first, so never bring in azolla without checking it. Clean the canals and put a screen at the water inlet. Then remove the mats by hand or with a net early, and take out every broken piece. If you need a herbicide, pick one by weed group and the age of your rice, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: How can I tell salvinia from azolla?
items.a: Look at the size and the hairs. Azolla is tiny, with small overlapping scale like leaves, and it often turns reddish in the sun. Salvinia leaves are bigger, round to heart shaped, and covered with stiff hairs. Each node also carries a brown, root like leaf that hangs in the water.
